sections.h2: How a Virginia tax sale works
sections.html:
The locality begins by suing in the circuit court of the county or city where the property sits. The suit enforces the lien for delinquent taxes and asks the court to sell the real estate (Va. Code 58.1-3967). Procedure follows the rules for a creditor's suit to sell real estate on a judgment lien, except where a statute says something different.

Everyone with an interest has to be named: lienors, anyone claiming title, and the beneficiary and trustees under a deed of trust. Title passes at the judicial sale free of those parties' claims, and former owners can claim surplus afterward.

sections.h2: When a property can be sold for delinquent taxes
sections.html:
The usual trigger is tax still delinquent on December 31 after the second anniversary of the date it came due. A property with a condemned structure, a nuisance, a derelict building, or a blighted declaration can be reached after the first anniversary instead (Va. Code 58.1-3965).

Real estate assessed at $100,000 or less gets different treatment. Once the court finds taxes delinquent on December 31 after the first anniversary, the property is deemed subject to sale at public auction after proper notice. Certain unpaid local lien costs for abatement or repair work the same way.

SituationEarliest sale trigger
Ordinary parcelDecember 31 after the second anniversary of the due date
Condemned, nuisance, derelict, or blightedDecember 31 after the first anniversary
Assessed at $100,000 or less (court finding)December 31 after the first anniversary

In a qualifying locality with unpaid abatement costs, the periods for the condemned and blighted categories can shrink to six months.

At least 30 days before starting court action, the collecting officer must send notice to the owner's last known address in the treasurer's records. If the property address differs and is a numbered, named street address, the notice goes there too. It tells the owner that a payment agreement of up to 72 months may be requested (Va. Code 58.1-3965).

The officer also publishes a list of the properties at least once in a local newspaper, again at least 30 days before the case is filed. Publication costs, the court's reasonable attorney fees, and title examination costs are added to what the owner owes, even when the owner pays before any case is filed.

If you move often or live out of state, keep the treasurer's records current. A notice mailed to an old address helps no one. An owner served only by publication may petition for a rehearing, but only for good cause and only within 90 days after the sale is confirmed.

sections.h2: How an owner can stop the sale
sections.html:
Pay everything owed before the sale date. An owner may redeem at any time up to the sale by paying the accumulated taxes, penalties, interest, reasonable attorney fees, and costs, including the pro rata cost of publication. Paying part of the balance does not redeem the property or stop the lawsuit (Va. Code 58.1-3965).

Heirs, devisees, successors, and assigns have the same right and redeem by paying into court before the sale date. Whoever pays taxes on the property gets a lien for the amount paid, with interest at six percent a year (Va. Code 58.1-3974).

The statute offers other options too:

  • The treasurer may suspend the sale under an installment agreement of up to 72 months, which must also cover current taxes as they come due.
  • A person who is not a party but claims ownership through a will or intestate succession can send written notice to the treasurer, who may suspend the case and ask the court to add that person as a party.
  • The court may refer the parties to a dispute resolution proceeding.

Miss a payment on an installment plan and the treasurer can void it on 15 days' written notice. The case then goes forward without repeating the notice, and no second plan is available for three years.

sections.h2: Heirs when the owner has died
sections.html:
Heirs have a path built in. A person who claims ownership by will or by intestate succession can notify the treasurer in writing, and the treasurer may suspend the action while seeking leave to add that person as a party. If the court finds the person holds an ownership interest, that person has 30 days to enter an installment agreement for the delinquent amounts, over no more than 72 months (Va. Code 58.1-3965).

An estate problem and a tax problem meet here. If probate has not started, the person with the strongest claim should contact both the circuit court clerk and the treasurer quickly. Our Virginia probate guide explains who can qualify.

Costs grow three ways. Penalty and interest keep accruing under the locality's ordinance, with interest capped at 10 percent a year at first and a higher ceiling in later years. The locality may also recover attorney or collection agency fees actually contracted for, up to 20 percent of the delinquent taxes and charges (Va. Code 58.1-3916).

The third is the lien itself. Real estate tax ranks ahead of every other lien and stays there until actual payment, so a buyer or lender cannot work around it, and any sale needs the tax paid from proceeds (Va. Code 58.1-3340). It covers rents for the current year as well.

The former owner and the heirs, devisees, successors, or assigns are entitled to what is left after taxes, penalties, interest, reasonable attorney fees, costs, and liens. The claimant carries the burden of proving entitlement. If no one claims the surplus within two years after the sale is confirmed, the clerk pays it to the locality. A governing body may grant relief by ordinance and pay a person who shows prior entitlement whatever amount it considers appropriate (Va. Code 58.1-3967).

The grantor's transfer tax of 50 cents per $500 does not apply when the grantor is a locality at a judicial sale of tax-delinquent property (Va. Code 58.1-802).

A private sale lets you pick the buyer and the timing, and the tax lien comes out of the proceeds, so the rest is yours. A judicial sale runs on the court's schedule, and surplus can take time and proof to claim. If the case grows, costs can also eat the equity in a house with a lien.

Each locality has its own treasurer's office and circuit court, so the list, the notices, and the fees depend on where the house stands. Ask the treasurer for a written payoff, ask the circuit court clerk whether a case has been filed, and compare that payoff to what a buyer is offering. A cash purchase can close quickly enough to beat a sale date, as long as the payoff and the title are in order.

faqs.q: Can I stop a tax sale by paying part of what I owe?
faqs.a: No. Partial payment does not redeem the property and does not suspend or end the court action. Redemption takes all taxes, penalties, interest, attorney fees, and costs, unless the treasurer agrees to an installment plan.

faqs.q: How long can a payment plan last?
faqs.a: Up to 72 months, and it must also keep current taxes paid as they come due. If you default, the treasurer can void the plan on 15 days' written notice.

faqs.q: Does the locality have to warn me before suing?
faqs.a: Yes. Notice must go out at least 30 days before court action, to the owner's address on file and to the property address if different, and a list of properties must be published in a local newspaper.

faqs.q: Do heirs have rights if the owner died?
faqs.a: Yes. Heirs, devisees, successors, and assigns may redeem before the sale, and a person claiming through a will or intestate succession can ask the treasurer to suspend the case.

faqs.q: Who gets the money if the property sells for more than the taxes?
faqs.a: The former owner and heirs, devisees, successors, or assigns, after taxes, fees, costs, and liens, if they prove entitlement within two years of confirmation. After that it goes to the locality.
